text.en: Asha asked how India talks with other countries. "Through foreign policy," said the teacher.

Foreign policy is how a country deals with others. India's foreign policy is guided by the principles of peace, non-alignment, respect for sovereignty and cooperation. Jawaharlal Nehru shaped its early form with the Panchsheel principles.
India follows the Non-Aligned Movement, supports the United Nations and works for disarmament and against colonialism and apartheid. It has good relations with neighbours and the world and believes in 'the world is one family'.
India stays strong with an independent policy, and its relations with major powers and its neighbours matter for trade and peace. The Ministry of External Affairs carries out the foreign policy.

It has good relations with neighbours and the world and believes in 'the world is one family'.
India stays strong with an independent policy, and its relations with major powers and its neighbours matter for trade and peace.
The Ministry of External Affairs carries out the foreign policy.
Independent India stepped onto the world stage in 1947 amid Cold War rivalry between the USA and USSR—choosing peace, autonomy and development over joining military camps.
Foreign policy reflects geography, history, economy, military strength and national values—India's Ministry of External Affairs coordinates diplomacy worldwide.

board.text: What shapes a nation's foreign policy?

text.en: Our Constitution itself sets a compass in Article 51 (Directive Principles): promote international peace, respect international law and settle disputes by arbitration.
First Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru championed Panchsheel—Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence—signed with China in 1954 as a model for global diplomacy.
The five Panchsheel principles are: mutual respect for sovereignty, mutual non-aggression, non-interference in internal affairs, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence.
In 1955 at the Bandung Conference in Indonesia, newly freed Asian and African nations built solidarity that led directly to the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961.
Founded by Nehru, Tito of Yugoslavia, Nasser of Egypt, Sukarno of Indonesia and Nkrumah of Ghana, NAM refused to join Cold War power blocs.

board.text: NAM founders: stay free of military blocs

text.en: Non-alignment never meant neutrality or isolation; it meant judging every global crisis independently on merit while fighting colonialism and South African apartheid.

board.text: NAM meant independent judgment, not isolation

text.en: True to 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam'—the world is one family—India strongly supports the United Nations, contributing prominently to UN peacekeeping missions worldwide.
On nuclear policy, India advocates verifiable global disarmament while maintaining 'Credible Minimum Deterrence' and a firm 'No First Use' pledge.

board.text: Nuclear policy: No First Use & disarmament

text.en: Within South Asia, India follows the Neighbourhood First policy alongside the earlier Gujral Doctrine of offering non-reciprocal goodwill to smaller neighbours.
After 1991 economic reforms, diplomacy expanded to 'Look East'—upgraded to 'Act East'—deepening trade, rail and sea links with ASEAN and East Asia.

board.text: 1991 onwards: Look East -> Act East Policy

text.en: Across the Indian Ocean, India champions SAGAR—Security and Growth for All in the Region—protecting sea lanes and supporting island nations in disasters.

board.text: SAGAR: Security & Growth in Indian Ocean

text.en: Westward, 'Link West' strengthens energy security, space and trade ties with Gulf nations and protects millions of Indian workers living there.
Today India practices multi-alignment: partnering simultaneously in BRICS and SCO alongside Quad (India, USA, Japan, Australia) and the G20.
India also acts as a voice for the Global South, sharing digital public goods like UPI, vaccines and solar power alliances.
Every foreign decision balances three goals: protecting territorial security, growing trade & technology for citizens at home, and building global peace.
Even disasters showcase Indian diplomacy: 'Vaccine Maitri' and rapid earthquake or cyclone rescue teams build lasting goodwill.
At home, Parliament debates treaties, embassies assist Indian students abroad, and the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) represents India daily.

board.text: How embassies & MEA serve citizens abroad

text.en: Note how India adapted across eras: non-alignment during the Cold War -> economic diplomacy after 1991 -> strategic multi-alignment in the 21st century.
Notice also the steady threads: sovereignty, anti-colonialism, Article 51 peace principles and global cooperation stay unchanged.
Summary chain: Panchsheel & Article 51 -> Non-Aligned independence -> Act East & Neighbourhood First -> confident G20 leadership.

board.text: Core values -> NAM -> Act East -> G20

text.en: Understanding foreign policy shows how thoughtful diplomacy protects a billion Indians while building a fairer, safer world.
